messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Leilani is a 67-year-old database administrator who has worked for the same county government for twenty-two years, a bastion of quiet order in a life that no longer feels like her own. It has been eight months since she ended her relationship with David, and nearly a year since the night that fractured her sense of safety. After her husband of forty years passed away, Leilani had been profoundly lonely. David had seemed like a gentle answer to that loneliness, until he wasn't. The arguments started small, but the final one was different. He had backed her into the corner of their bedroom, his voice a low growl, his eyes locked on hers with an intensity that felt like it was pinning her to the wall. She remembers the floral pattern of the wallpaper behind her head, the feel of the plaster against her shoulders. When she had tried to look away, to break the terrifying hold of his gaze, he had grabbed her face, forcing her to look at him as he spoke. The physical blows that followed felt almost secondary to the violation of being held captive by his eyes.

In the months since, Leilani has engineered a life devoid of the possibility of that kind of contact. At work, during team meetings, she keeps her laptop open and her gaze fixed on the screen, even when she isn't the one presenting. Her colleagues have started to see her as aloof, even disinterested. She feels their misjudgment like a low-grade fever but is certain that looking up, meeting their friendly gazes, would be unbearable. She has come to believe her reactions are a sign of profound weakness; that a stronger person would have moved on by now. This thought circles endlessly: "My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper." The woman who once mentored junior staff and organized office potlucks now eats lunch alone at her desk, her world shrunk to the predictable logic of SQL queries.

Her home, once a sanctuary, has become a place to dread the coming of darkness. Sleep offers no escape, only a gateway to reliving that night. To combat this, Leilani stays awake until she is on the verge of collapse. She watches old black-and-white movies until three or four in the morning, the television’s gray light a weak shield against the memories that pool in the quiet of the house. She only allows herself to sleep when the first hints of dawn appear, believing that the dark is what holds the danger. This chronic exhaustion has seeped into every corner of her life, leaving her feeling brittle and disconnected from the competent, energetic woman she used to be. When she catches her reflection, the face looking back is a stranger's. The thought is a constant, quiet hum: "I feel like I don't know myself anymore."

Perhaps the most painful change has been her relationship with her family. Her daughter brings the grandchildren over for Sunday dinner, a tradition Leilani once cherished. Now, she feels a surge of panic when her seven-year-old grandson runs toward her for a hug. She flinches and turns away before he can touch her, a small, involuntary movement that stops him in his tracks. The hurt in his eyes is a fresh wound every time. She knows it's not him, it's any touch, but she cannot explain it. The shame that follows is immense, cementing her belief that there is something fundamentally broken inside her. The only explanation that makes sense to her is that she invited the abuse, that some core part of her is flawed. "There is something wrong with me as a person," she concludes, a verdict she delivers to herself in the lonely hours before dawn. It was after her grandson stopped trying to hug her altogether that Leilani finally made the call to seek help, terrified that the person she used to be was gone for good and that she was doomed to push away everyone she had left.
